Avicenna, or Ibn Sina, was a Persian physician and philosopher, born near Bukhara around 980 and dead in Hamadan in 1037. He is one of the greatest thinkers of the Islamic Golden Age, and his books were taught in both the Islamic world and Europe for centuries.

He grew up in the Samanid capital. As a teenager he cured the Samanid ruler and was allowed into the royal library, where he read widely. When the Samanid state fell in 999 he left and spent the rest of his life moving between the courts of Iranian rulers, often as physician and sometimes as vizier. He is said to have refused a summons to the court of Mahmud of Ghazni.

He wrote, by tradition, some 450 works, of which about 240 survive. The two best known:

  • The Canon of Medicine, a medical encyclopedia. In Latin translation it became a standard text in European universities and was still used in the 1600s.
  • The Book of Healing, a vast encyclopedia of philosophy and science.

In philosophy he built on Aristotle and the Greek works translated in Baghdad, and he became the leading voice of that school in the Muslim world. His ideas on the soul and on being influenced Christian scholars such as Thomas Aquinas.

He wrote mostly in Arabic, the scholarly language of his day, but also in Persian. He belongs with al-Khwarizmi and al-Biruni among the scholars from Central Asia who shaped world science.
